title: Just one question
subtitle: Deutsch's algorithm: finding out a global property of a function by querying it only once.

steps.title: The black box
body: Someone hands you a black box that computes a function f from one bit to one bit. It's either constant (f(0) = f(1)) or balanced (f(0) ≠ f(1)). Which is it?
Classically, there's no way around it: you have to query f(0) and f(1). Two queries.
In 1985, David Deutsch showed that a quantum computer can do it with one.

steps.title: Oracles as circuits
body: The box becomes a two-qubit gate: |x⟩|y⟩ → |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩. The qubit x is the question; f(x) is added (XOR) into y.
If f(x) = x (balanced), the oracle is a CNOT. If f(x) = 1 (constant), it's an X on y.
The trick: prepare y in |−⟩. Then adding f(x) into y doesn't change y — it only multiplies the state by (−1)^f(x). The answer “kicks back” into the phase of x: that's phase kickback.

steps.title: Query the balanced oracle
steps.goal: The fixed oracle is a CNOT (f(x) = x). y starts in |1⟩. Build the circuit so that x ends up in |1⟩ — the “balanced” signal.
hints: Before the oracle: put x in superposition and turn y from |1⟩ into |−⟩.
After the oracle: an H on x turns the phase into a result.
steps.success: A single query! On the sphere, look: y didn't even move with the oracle, but the arrow of x went to the other side of the equator — the answer ended up in the phase.

steps.question: Same circuit, but now the oracle is constant (f(x) = 1, an X on y). What's the chance of measuring x = 1?
steps.explain: Zero. With a constant oracle, both branches of x get the same phase (a global, invisible phase) and the last H brings x back to |0⟩. Result 0 = constant, 1 = balanced.

steps.question: What's the essential ingredient that makes the algorithm work?

options.text: The quantum computer tests f(0) and f(1) in parallel and reads both.
options.why: It does “query both” in superposition, but a measurement only gives one result. Without interference, nothing useful could be extracted.

options.text: Phase kickback + interference: f(x) becomes a phase on x, and the final H turns the phase difference into a result.
options.why: Exactly. It's the same pattern as many algorithms: prepare a superposition, mark with phase, interfere.
It has nothing to do with physical speed: it's about how many queries are needed.

steps.title: The first quantum algorithm
steps.text: Deutsch's 1985 paper also described the universal quantum computer. In 1992, with Richard Jozsa, he generalized the problem to n bits: the Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm solves with 1 query what a deterministic classical algorithm could need up to 2ⁿ⁻¹ + 1 queries for. With randomness, classical does much better — but the idea paved the way for Simon, Shor and Grover.

takeaways: Quantum oracles are reversible gates: |x⟩|y⟩ → |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩.
With the target in |−⟩, the oracle's answer becomes a phase on the input register (phase kickback).
Superposition + phase + interference: the general recipe of quantum algorithms.
